subsection: 6. France: the Third Republic, 1920-1940, and the Vichy state

notes.h: How the Third Republic worked
notes.b: The Third Republic was France's parliamentary democracy from 1870 to 1940. Its institutions and parties explain why so much of the politics of the 1920s and 1930s looked the way it did.
points: The Republic was proclaimed in 1870, after France's defeat by Prussia, and its constitutional laws date from 1875. Democracy here means government by elected representatives answerable to the voters, with free elections, parties and civil rights, although only men could vote.
Parliament had two houses: an elected Chamber of Deputies and an indirectly elected Senate, which could block laws, so reforms needed to pass both. Women had no vote until 1944-45.

The President, elected for seven years by the Chamber and Senate meeting together, had a largely ceremonial role. Real power lay with the Prime Minister (called the President of the Council) and the ministers.
Governments needed a majority in the Chamber and fell when they lost a vote, so ministers lived at the mercy of the deputies.
No single party ever won a majority, so every government was a coalition. The right was made up of conservative and Catholic groups, and the Radical Party stood in the centre-left.

The Radical Party, anticlerical (opposed to the Church's influence) and strong among small-town and rural voters, was the hinge of most coalitions because governments needed its votes whether they leaned left or right. It was the largest force in most governments of the 1920s and early 1930s.
The left consisted of the Socialists (the SFIO) and, from 1920, the Communists (the PCF), founded at the Congress of Tours in December 1920 after a split in the Socialist party.

French society was deeply divided: left against right, Catholic against secular (anticlerical) France, workers against employers, Paris against the provinces. These divisions shaped every crisis of the period, because each camp distrusted the other's government.
notes.tip: Ordinary Level short accounts of the Third Republic expect the constitution, frequent changes of government, the Bloc National, the Cartel and Poincaré. Start with how the system worked and then give named evidence.

notes.h: The legacy of the war and the Bloc National, 1919-1924
notes.b: France won the First World War but paid heavily for it, and its politics after 1919 were dominated by the demand that Germany pay. The first post-war government, the Bloc National, was built around that aim.
points: About 1.4 million French soldiers were killed in 1914-1918, and the north-east, where much of the fighting took place, was devastated, with many villages and farms destroyed. A falling birth rate and heavy war debts added to the damage.
Alsace-Lorraine returned to France by the Treaty of Versailles in 1919. Even so, France felt a deep fear of Germany, so it wanted the treaty enforced in full.

Reconstruction of the devastated areas was financed by borrowing, in the expectation that German reparations (payments for war damage) would repay the loans. The slogan of the early 1920s, 'Germany will pay' ('L'Allemagne paiera'), summed up this hope.
The Bloc National, a coalition of conservative, centre and Catholic parties, won the November 1919 election and governed until 1924. It took a firm line on Germany and against the left.
Clemenceau left politics, his career ended, after he was defeated in the presidential election of January 1920 by Paul Deschanel.
Budget deficits, large debts and a falling franc marked the early and mid 1920s. This made the government's reliance on German payments a financial gamble as well as a political one.
notes.tip: In the essay on the problems France faced between 1920 and 1940, give the war legacy and finance their own section, with named evidence, and say whether the problem was overcome.

notes.h: Poincaré and the occupation of the Ruhr, 1923-1925
notes.b: When Germany fell behind with reparations, France chose force. The result showed the limits of French power and left it short of friends.
points: Raymond Poincaré was Prime Minister from January 1922 to June 1924 and took a hard line towards Germany, which suited the parties of the Bloc National.
In January 1923, after Germany defaulted on reparations (failed to pay what was due), French and Belgian troops occupied the Ruhr, a German industrial area.
Germany answered with passive resistance, refusing to co-operate with the occupiers. Britain disapproved openly and refused to take part.
The Dawes Plan of 1924 reorganised German payments, so the French troops were no longer needed and were withdrawn by 1925.

The occupation brought some payments, but also isolation, cost and a weaker franc, so it ended without securing full reparations. There is more on the German side, including hyperinflation, in the notes on Weimar Germany.
notes.tip: Use the Ruhr as named evidence that the war legacy was not overcome by force: some payments, but isolation, cost and a weaker franc. Say Britain disapproved; do not claim more than that.

notes.h: Security and foreign policy in the 1920s
notes.b: While governments argued about money, French foreign policy pursued one aim: protection against a revival of German power.
points: France made an alliance with Poland in 1921 and a treaty with Czechoslovakia in 1924, to gain friends against Germany in eastern Europe.
Aristide Briand was Foreign Minister for most of the years 1925 to 1932 and favoured agreement with Germany rather than force, in contrast to Poincaré's hard line.
The Locarno treaties of 1925, which aimed to keep the peace in western Europe, and the Kellogg-Briand Pact of 1928, in which states renounced war, were his best-known achievements.
Briand shared the 1926 Nobel Peace Prize with the German statesman Stresemann.
France also decided in this period to build a fortified line along the German border, the Maginot Line, as a further guarantee of security.

notes.h: The Cartel des Gauches and the Poincaré franc, 1924-1929
notes.b: Voters turned left in 1924, but a financial crisis undid the new government. Poincaré's return then restored confidence and gave France a few calm, prosperous years.
points: The Cartel des Gauches, a coalition of Radicals and Socialists, won the May 1924 election, and Édouard Herriot, a Radical, was Prime Minister from June 1924 to April 1925.

The Cartel fell in April 1925 after a run on the franc (people rushing to sell francs) and a financial crisis. It was called the 'wall of money': banks and investors had lost confidence in a left-wing government.
A run of short governments followed in the next years, and the franc crisis of July 1926 brought Poincaré back at the head of a Government of National Union.
Poincaré raised taxes and cut spending, which restored confidence, so the franc was stabilised in practice by late 1926.
The 'Poincaré franc' was fixed in law in June 1928 at about one-fifth of its 1914 gold value. The late 1920s were prosperous, and Poincaré retired in July 1929 because of ill health.
notes.tip: The Poincaré franc is your evidence that the financial problem was overcome in the late 1920s, while the Cartel's fall shows how fragile governments were. Use both in a 'how far overcome' essay.

notes.h: Why governments changed so often
notes.b: Governments in the Third Republic were short-lived, which made steady policy difficult. Several features of the system, working together, explain why.
points: There were many parties and no majority party, so governments were fragile coalitions that lasted only as long as every partner agreed.
The Radicals switched between left and right partners, so withdrawing their support could topple a government quickly.
The Chamber held frequent votes of no confidence, and governments changed very often, many lasting only months. Ministers were often replaced after a few months in office.
The President had the power to dissolve the Chamber, but it was not used after 1877, so deputies could bring down governments without facing an election themselves.
The Senate blocked reforms, so reforming governments lost momentum, and financial crises, especially in 1924-26, brought governments down.

The President's role was largely ceremonial, so policy was decided by the Prime Minister and the parliamentary majority, and when the majority broke up there was no one else to hold the government together.
notes.tip: For 'why was the Republic unstable', link cause to result, for example the Senate refusing Blum emergency powers in 1937 and so ending his government. Do not give a total number of governments.

notes.h: The Depression in France: late arrival and deflation
notes.b: France's economy was less affected by the Depression at first than Britain's or Germany's, but the slump arrived later and was prolonged by government policy.
points: France's economy rested on small family farms and small family firms, and the country held large gold reserves, which cushioned it against the immediate effects of the Wall Street Crash.

The slump hit in earnest from 1931, with industrial production falling sharply. It then lasted longer than in Britain or Germany, and recovery was slow until the late 1930s. Farmers and small businesses suffered most.
Official unemployment stayed lower than in Britain or Germany, partly because foreign workers left and some unemployed returned to the land. It still remained a serious problem.

Governments kept the franc at its 1928 gold value, and France led the 'gold bloc' of countries that stayed on gold. To defend the currency they used deflation, cutting spending, wages and prices, which deepened the slump and hurt industry and farming.
Pierre Laval, Prime Minister from June 1935 to January 1936, issued decree-laws in 1935 that cut public spending and salaries, so the policy of deflation continued.
The franc was devalued (its gold value lowered) only under the Popular Front in autumn 1936, after which exports recovered slightly.

The left (Radicals and Socialists) won the May 1932 election and Herriot was Prime Minister again, but governments fell in quick succession. Contempt for parliament and 'the politicians' grew, which prepared the ground for the leagues.
notes.tip: Say that the Depression came late but lasted long, and that deflation was a policy choice that made it worse. Do not quote unemployment figures.

notes.h: The leagues
notes.b: As faith in parliament fell, leagues offered an alternative. These were anti-parliamentary, nationalist and mostly right-wing movements.
points: Action française was founded in 1899 and led by Charles Maurras. It was monarchist and anti-Semitic, had opposed the republic since before 1914, and its street militants were called the Camelots du Roi.
The Jeunesses Patriotes were led by Pierre Taittinger, and the Solidarité française was funded by the perfume maker François Coty, so the leagues had wealthy backers as well as street militants.
The Croix-de-Feu was a veterans' league led by Colonel François de La Rocque. It was the largest league, with hundreds of thousands of members by 1936.
Francisme, led by Marcel Bucard, was a smaller group that was openly fascist, which made it different from the larger leagues that claimed only to defend the nation.

Economic hardship and fear of war split French opinion into left and right camps, so the leagues found support on the right while Communists and Socialists gained from the unity forged after February 1934.

Historians disagree on how far the leagues threatened democracy. René Rémond argued that they belonged to France's traditional right, while Zeev Sternhell (Neither Right nor Left, 1983) argued that fascist ideas had deep roots in France.
After the leagues were dissolved in 1936, the Croix-de-Feu re-formed as the Parti Social Français, which grew into a large party.
notes.tip: Be ready to say whether the leagues were fascist, using both Rémond and Sternhell. Do not confuse Action française (monarchist, Maurras) with the Croix-de-Feu (veterans, La Rocque). Do not quote a membership figure other than 'hundreds of thousands'.

notes.h: The Stavisky affair and the riots of 6 February 1934
notes.b: A financial scandal in January 1934 gave the leagues their chance. The riot that followed brought down a government and pushed the left to unite.
points: Alexandre Stavisky was a swindler with political protection who sold worthless bonds through the municipal pawnshop (the Crédit municipal) of Bayonne.
He was found shot dead in January 1934. The police called it suicide, but left and right both suspected he had been silenced, and the affair suggested corruption reaching into the Radical Party.
The scandal forced the resignation of the Radical Prime Minister Camille Chautemps in January 1934, and the leagues used it to attack the republic as corrupt.
The new Prime Minister, Édouard Daladier, dismissed Jean Chiappe, the Paris Prefect of Police, who was favoured by the right. This angered the right further.

On 6 February 1934 the leagues, including the Croix-de-Feu, Action française and the Solidarité française, and veterans' groups marched on the Chamber of Deputies. Police opened fire and about 15 people were killed and over a thousand injured.
Daladier resigned on 7 February, the first government brought down by street violence. A government of national union under Gaston Doumergue, with Pétain as War Minister, was formed to restore order.
The left read 6 February as an attempted fascist coup. It responded with a general strike and mass demonstration on 12 February 1934, which led to left unity.
notes.tip: Stavisky and 6 February are named evidence for the problem of division and instability. For the Popular Front, say it formed in reaction to 6 February.

notes.h: The Popular Front: formation and the 1936 election
notes.b: Fear of fascism did what years of argument had not, and brought Socialists, Communists and Radicals together. Their alliance, the Popular Front, won power in 1936.
points: The Socialist-Communist unity-of-action pact of July 1934 was possible because the Comintern, the international body of Communist parties directed from Moscow, had reversed the Communists' hostility to other left parties. Its Seventh Congress confirmed the popular front line in 1935.
The Radicals joined in 1935, shown at the mass rally of 14 July 1935, and a joint programme followed in January 1936. The slogan was 'Bread, Peace and Liberty' ('Pain, Paix, Liberté').
The Popular Front won a majority in the elections of 26 April and 3 May 1936, and Léon Blum became Prime Minister on 4 June 1936. Socialists and Radicals sat in the cabinet.
The Communists supported the government in parliament but took no ministries, so they should not be listed as ministers.
Blum was the first Socialist and the first Jewish Prime Minister, but not the first left-of-centre one, because Herriot, a Radical, had led the Cartel in 1924.
Blum was attacked by the anti-Semitic right and was beaten up by Action française supporters in February 1936.
Three women became under-secretaries, Cécile Brunschvicg, Irène Joliot-Curie and Suzanne Lacore, although women could not yet vote.
notes.tip: Give the formation dates in order: the Socialist-Communist pact in July 1934, the Radicals in 1935, the programme in January 1936. Do not give July 1935 as the founding date.

notes.h: The strike wave and the Matignon Agreements, 1936
notes.b: Workers expected a Popular Front government to improve their lives, and they pressed the point with strikes. The employers gave way, and the Matignon Agreements and the June laws were the biggest social gains of the period.
points: The strikes began in May 1936 (from about 11 May), before Blum took office. The main wave and the factory occupations came after he formed his government on 4 June, and they peaked in early-to-mid June.
Many were sit-down strikes, in which workers occupied their factories instead of leaving them, and about two million workers were out at the height of the wave.

The pressure of the wave pushed the employers into the Matignon Agreements, reached on 7-8 June 1936 in the middle of the wave to end it. They were signed at the Hôtel Matignon, the Prime Minister's residence, with Blum chairing the talks between employers and unions.
The agreements gave wage rises of about 7 to 15 per cent, union recognition (the right of unions to represent workers), collective agreements and elected workers' delegates.
Laws that month brought in the 40-hour week and two weeks' paid holiday, which meant that for the first time many workers could take a holiday.
notes.tip: Do not say the strikes were over before Blum took office, or that two million were out before it: the main wave followed his government's formation on 4 June, and Matignon was reached in the middle of it.

notes.h: Other Popular Front reforms
notes.b: Beyond Matignon, the government used its majority to reshape the economy, farming, schools and leisure, and to deal with the leagues.
points: The leagues were dissolved in June 1936, because the government feared the threat they had shown on 6 February 1934.
The Wheat Office was set up in 1936 to stabilise farm prices, which helped farmers hurt by deflation, for example wheat growers.
The state gained greater control of the Bank of France, and the arms industry was part-nationalised (partly taken into state ownership).
The school-leaving age was raised to 14 in 1936 by the education minister Jean Zay.
Léo Lagrange, under-secretary for sport and leisure, developed a leisure and sport policy that included cheap rail tickets for holidays.
A rearmament programme began in September 1936, and the franc was devalued in autumn 1936.
The plans for public works spending were limited by financial pressure and capital flight.

notes.h: Problems of the Popular Front
notes.b: The Popular Front's gains were soon eroded by economic trouble, and the Spanish Civil War split the coalition itself.
points: Capital fled abroad because investors distrusted the government, and rising prices ate up the wage gains of workers.
Industrial output was slow to recover, and the 40-hour week limited production, including the production of arms.

Blum adopted a policy of non-intervention in the Spanish Civil War in August 1936. This angered the Communists and much of his own party, but Britain backed non-intervention and the Radicals opposed intervening, so he feared splitting the coalition and the country.
Roger Salengro, the Interior Minister, killed himself in November 1936 after a campaign against him in the right-wing press.

The anti-Semitic right hated Blum, and a phrase attributed to parts of the right said they preferred Hitler to Blum. The origin of the phrase is unclear, so do not treat it as anyone's recorded words.
notes.tip: A good answer on why the Popular Front failed combines economic problems (capital flight, prices, the 40-hour week) with the split over Spain. Treat the Spanish war only as it affected France.

notes.h: Decline and end of the Popular Front, 1937-1938
notes.b: Economic pressure and the Senate's opposition ended the Popular Front's reforming period. Its social gains were then undone one by one.
points: Blum announced a pause in reform in February 1937, because financial pressure made further spending impossible.
He resigned in June 1937 when the Senate refused him emergency financial powers. Governments under Chautemps followed.
Blum led a brief second government in March and April 1938, and Daladier became Prime Minister in April 1938 (he held office until March 1940), which ended the coalition.
The finance minister Paul Reynaud's decree-laws of November 1938 undid the 40-hour week.
The general strike of 30 November 1938 failed, and its failure ended the Popular Front era.
notes.tip: Link cause to result: the Senate refusing financial powers ended Blum's government. Ordinary Level answers on the Popular Front should cover formation after 6 February, Blum, Matignon gains and why it failed.

notes.h: The Maginot Line and defensive military thinking
notes.b: France's defences in the 1930s reflected memories of the First World War and a fear of losing another generation of young men. The result was a defensive strategy with fatal weaknesses.
points: The Maginot Line was named after André Maginot, the War Minister. A law funding it passed in January 1930, and it was built mainly in the 1930s, so it was funded from 1930 and built mainly in the 1930s. It was very expensive.
It was a system of concrete forts and underground works along the Franco-German border, designed to hold an invader while the army mobilised.
It reflected defensive thinking after Verdun and the shortage of manpower, because France could not afford the huge casualties of attacking again.
It did not extend along the Belgian border, because Belgium was an ally until it declared neutrality in 1936. It was also weak opposite the Ardennes, a wooded region thought unsuitable for tanks.
The army's doctrine was slow, methodical and defensive. Tanks were spread among infantry units instead of being concentrated.
De Gaulle's book of 1934, Vers l'armée de métier (in English The Army of the Future), argued for a professional armoured force. It was ignored.
notes.tip: Examiners ask why France fell and expect the Maginot Line gap, tank tactics and command. Say the Line was very expensive, but give no cost figure, and do not give a build date other than funded from 1930 and built mainly in the 1930s.

notes.h: French foreign policy in the 1930s
notes.b: As Hitler's Germany rearmed, France looked for allies but did not act alone. Its caution helped to make war more likely.
points: France signed the Franco-Soviet Pact in May 1935, because it hoped for an ally against Germany.
When Hitler remilitarised the Rhineland on 7 March 1936, France took no action, and its reliance on Britain grew.

Daladier signed the Munich Agreement on 29-30 September 1938, which showed how far France followed Britain's policy of appeasement. There is more on Hitler's side and the causes of war in the notes on the Nazi state and Hitler's foreign policy.

notes.h: Declaring war and the German attack, 1939-1940
notes.b: France declared war in September 1939 but did little fighting for eight months. When the German attack came in May 1940, the French plan collapsed within weeks.
points: France declared war on Germany on 3 September 1939, after the invasion of Poland. During the Phoney War (the drôle de guerre) there was little fighting, and the army under General Maurice Gamelin, the commander-in-chief, waited behind the Maginot Line.
The Communist Party was banned in September 1939 after the Nazi-Soviet Pact, which the Communists had to defend. Paul Reynaud replaced Daladier as Prime Minister in March 1940.
The German attack began on 10 May 1940. Gamelin and Pétain thought the Ardennes forest difficult terrain for tanks, so the main French and British forces moved into Belgium on the Dyle plan.
German armoured divisions came through the Ardennes and crossed the Meuse at Sedan on 13 May and reached the Channel coast at Abbeville on 20 May, cutting off the northern armies.
Maxime Weygand replaced Gamelin on 19 May. The British Expeditionary Force and many French troops, about 338,000 Allied troops in all, were evacuated from Dunkirk between 26 May and 4 June.
There is more on blitzkrieg and the general course of the war in the notes on the Second World War.
notes.tip: For the fall of France, give the sequence with dates: Ardennes, Sedan on 13 May, the Channel coast on 20 May, Dunkirk, Paris, Pétain and the armistice.

notes.h: Collapse and the armistice, June 1940
notes.b: Once the northern armies were cut off, resistance collapsed. Within six weeks the government had asked for peace and the Republic was at an end.
points: Italy declared war on France on 10 June 1940. Paris was declared an open city (undefended) and occupied on 14 June, and millions of civilians fled south in the 'exodus'.
The government left Paris for Bordeaux, and Reynaud resigned on 16 June. Pétain became Prime Minister and asked Germany for an armistice on 17 June.

The armistice was signed with Germany on 22 June 1940 at Compiègne, in the same railway carriage as the 1918 armistice, so that Germany's humiliation of 1918 was reversed. A separate armistice with Italy followed on 24 June.
France was divided into an occupied zone, the north and the Atlantic coast, about three-fifths of the country, and an unoccupied zone in the south. Alsace-Lorraine was in practice annexed by Germany.
France had to pay the costs of occupation, at first 400 million francs a day, and prisoners of war were to stay in Germany.
The armistice army was limited to 100,000 men, and the fleet was to be disarmed but kept by France.
About 1.8 million French soldiers were taken prisoner in 1940, and well over a million were still in Germany years later.
notes.tip: Ordinary Level answers need the dates of 22 June and 10 July 1940. Do not confuse the armistice with Germany (22 June) with the one with Italy (24 June). Give no figure for French dead.

notes.h: The vote of 10 July 1940 and the end of the Third Republic
notes.b: The Third Republic did not fall to a coup. Its own parliament voted away its powers, which makes 10 July 1940 a key date in the story of democracy in France.
points: After the armistice the government settled at Vichy, a spa town in the unoccupied zone, in July 1940.

On 10 July 1940 the National Assembly, the Chamber and Senate meeting together in the Grand Casino at Vichy, voted by 569 to 80, with about 20 abstentions, to give full powers to Marshal Philippe Pétain to draw up a new constitution.
The vote did not itself create the Vichy regime. The next day, 11 July, Pétain's constitutional acts made him Head of the French State.

The order of events is therefore armistice (22 June), vote (10 July), Head of State (11 July). The Third Republic had survived the Depression and the leagues, but it ended by its own parliament's vote.
notes.tip: Keep the order straight: armistice on 22 June, the vote on 10 July, Head of State on 11 July. Say that the vote gave full powers to draw up a constitution, and that democracy ended by parliament's own vote.

notes.h: Why France fell
notes.b: The speed of the defeat shocked contemporaries and has been argued over ever since. Explanations fall into two schools, military and political.
points: Military explanations stress the army's slow defensive doctrine, slow command and communications, and the gamble that the Ardennes was unsuitable for tanks. German air power and surprise also mattered.

France had roughly as many tanks as Germany, but it spread many of them among infantry units instead of concentrating them in armoured divisions as Germany did, so the Germans could break through at one point.
The Maginot Line did not extend along the Belgian frontier or through the Ardennes, so the Germans simply went round it.
Ernest May (Strange Victory, 2000) stresses poor intelligence, slow command and German skill rather than moral failure.
Political and moral explanations stress instability, division, defeatism and 'decadence' (a decline in the nation's will). The historian Jean-Baptiste Duroselle took this view in La Décadence (1979).
Marc Bloch, a historian and army officer, wrote the contemporary witness account Strange Defeat in 1940 (published 1946). He later joined the Resistance and was shot by the Germans in 1944.
Contemporaries blamed the political decadence of the Third Republic, and Vichy used that explanation. Today most historians stress the military failures of May 1940.
notes.tip: Ordinary Level answers need the Maginot Line gap, tank tactics and command. Higher answers should name the two schools and give a view. Do not claim France had more or better tanks than Germany.

notes.h: Philippe Pétain
notes.b: Pétain was the most admired soldier in France in 1940 and became the ruler of the Vichy state. His reputation has fallen from saviour to collaborator.
points: Pétain was born in 1856 and became known as the 'victor of Verdun' for his part in the battle of 1916, which gave him huge prestige.
He was War Minister in 1934, in Doumergue's government, and ambassador to Franco's Spain in 1939.
He became Prime Minister in June 1940 at the age of 84, asked for the armistice, and was Head of the French State from 1940 to 1944.
He was taken to Sigmaringen in Germany in 1944 and was later tried in France. He was sentenced to death in August 1945, but de Gaulle commuted the sentence to life imprisonment, and he died in 1951.
Many saw him in 1940 as a saviour who would shield France, because he had been a hero in 1916.
Historians now judge him a collaborator who bore responsibility for persecution under his regime.

notes.h: Charles de Gaulle
notes.b: De Gaulle began 1940 as a little-known general and ended the war as the leader of liberated France. He also built the image of France that lasted for decades.
points: De Gaulle was born in 1890 and argued in the 1930s for armoured warfare, which was later shown to be the German method, but his ideas were ignored.
He commanded the 4th Armoured Division in May 1940, and became Under-Secretary of State for War in Reynaud's government from early June 1940.
His appeal of 18 June 1940 led to the Free French, and he led the Provisional Government from 1944. A Vichy court sentenced him to death in his absence in 1940, so his regime was a rival to Vichy.
He resigned in January 1946, and the Fourth Republic's constitution was approved by referendum in October 1946.
He built the post-war image of a France united in resistance, an image later historians challenged.

notes.h: Léon Blum
notes.b: Blum led the Popular Front government of 1936 and was the target of the anti-Semitic right. Vichy then put him on trial for the defeat.
points: Blum was born in 1872 and was a Socialist leader. He was Prime Minister in 1936-37 and briefly in 1938.
He was the first Socialist and the first Jewish Prime Minister, and was attacked by the anti-Semitic right, which beat him up in February 1936.
Vichy tried him at Riom, with Daladier and Gamelin, in a trial that opened in 1942 and was suspended when it embarrassed the regime.
He was held by the Germans from 1943 to 1945, near Buchenwald, and survived.

notes.h: Pierre Laval
notes.b: Laval held office under both the Third Republic and Vichy, and he is remembered above all as the man of collaboration.
points: Laval was born in 1883 and was Prime Minister in 1931-32 and 1935-36, so he led governments under the Third Republic as well as under Vichy.
His 1935 decree-laws cut spending and salaries, and the Hoare-Laval Pact of December 1935 concerned Abyssinia.
He became Pétain's deputy in 1940, but he was dismissed in December 1940. Admiral Darlan, not Laval, led the Vichy government in 1941.
He returned as head of government from April 1942 until 1944, and was executed in October 1945 after being convicted of treason.

notes.h: The French State and the National Revolution
notes.b: Pétain's regime rejected the Republic and its values. It called itself the French State and set out to remake France through what it called the National Revolution.
points: The regime renamed the state the French State (the État français). Pétain, aged 84, held executive and legislative power, and there was no parliament and there were no elections.

The capital was the spa town of Vichy. The regime governed all France in law, except Alsace-Lorraine, and was based in the unoccupied zone, but the Germans ruled the occupied zone directly through their military administration.

Instead of a single party, Vichy relied on the Legion of French Combatants, a veterans' organisation founded in August 1940. A cult of Pétain grew, with portraits and the song 'Maréchal, nous voilà!'.
Vichy's own press and radio supported the National Revolution, and its youth organisations, including the youth camps (Chantiers de la jeunesse), aimed to instil discipline and loyalty to Pétain.
The National Revolution blamed the defeat on the Republic, the left, the Popular Front and 'anti-French' groups, so it presented defeat as a punishment for decadence.
The motto 'Travail, Famille, Patrie' (Work, Family, Fatherland) replaced the republican 'Liberté, Égalité, Fraternite'.
It favoured the Catholic Church, the family and large families, women's place in the home, and a return to the land and rural life.
notes.tip: A short account of Vichy should give how it was created, the National Revolution and its motto, the Legion and at least three named policies. Do not confuse the Legion (1940) with the Milice (1943).

notes.h: Repression and control under Vichy
notes.b: Vichy was an authoritarian regime that silenced opposition and punished groups it blamed for the defeat.
points: The trade union confederations were dissolved and strikes were banned. The Labour Charter of October 1941 replaced the unions, so workers lost the rights won in 1936.
Freemasons, Communists and Jews were excluded from public life or persecuted, because the regime held them responsible for France's decline.
De Gaulle was sentenced to death in his absence in 1940.
The Riom trial of Blum, Daladier and Gamelin opened in February 1942, to blame the Republic's leaders for the defeat, but it was suspended in April 1942 when it embarrassed the regime.

notes.h: State collaboration and why Vichy collaborated
notes.b: Collaboration means co-operation with the occupying power. In France there was state collaboration by the Vichy government, and collaborationism, the open support for Nazism of fascist groups, was a separate phenomenon.
points: On 24 October 1940 Pétain met Hitler at Montoire, and on 30 October he announced in a broadcast: 'I enter today on the path of collaboration.'
Laval was dismissed on 13 December 1940, and Admiral François Darlan headed the government from February 1941 to April 1942.
Laval returned as head of government in April 1942 and in a broadcast in June 1942 said: 'I wish for a German victory.' This led to ever closer co-operation with Germany.

The British attack on the French fleet at Mers-el-Kébir in Algeria on 3 July 1940, to stop it falling into German hands, killed about 1,300 French sailors. It fed anti-British feeling and helped Vichy.
Vichy hoped for a better place in a German-dominated Europe, wanted the release of prisoners, saw a chance to carry out the National Revolution, and was anti-communist.
Defenders argued that Pétain acted as a 'shield' protecting the French from harsher German rule, whereas critics said Vichy collaborated willingly.

notes.h: The burden of occupation
notes.b: The occupation touched daily life in every part of France. It brought hardship and then, in 1942, ended Vichy's limited independence.
points: France had to pay the costs of the German occupation, set at 400 million francs a day at first, and its food, raw materials and industrial output were directed to Germany.
Rationing, queues, shortages and the black market (illegal trading at high prices) affected daily life, because so much was sent to Germany.
Well over a million French prisoners of war remained in Germany for years, so thousands of families lacked fathers and sons.
In 1942 the relève was announced in June: skilled workers went to Germany in return for the release of prisoners. It was voluntary and a failure.
After the Allied landings in French North Africa on 8 November 1942 (Operation Torch), the Germans occupied the southern zone on 11 November, so the 'free' zone ended.
The fleet was scuttled (sunk by its own crews) at Toulon on 27 November 1942, so that Germany could not seize it. Vichy lost what independence it had left.
notes.tip: Distinguish the voluntary relève of 1942 from the compulsory STO of 1943. For the civilians question, cover occupation, zones, rationing, prisoners of war, the STO, persecution, the Milice and reprisals.

notes.h: Collaborationists
notes.b: Some French people went further than the Vichy government, and wanted a fascist France allied to Nazi Germany. They are called collaborationists.
points: These were Paris-based fascist parties, more pro-Nazi than Vichy itself.
Jacques Doriot, an ex-Communist turned fascist, led the Parti Populaire Français, founded in 1936.
Marcel Deat led the Rassemblement National Populaire, founded in 1941.
The Legion of French Volunteers against Bolshevism, founded in 1941, fought on the Eastern Front, so it was an armed force of collaboration.
notes.tip: Keep the organisations apart: the Legion of French Combatants (1940, veterans), the Legion of French Volunteers (1941, fought in Russia) and the Milice (1943). Doriot's PPF was not the Croix-de-Feu.

notes.h: Anti-Jewish laws and deportations
notes.b: Vichy persecuted Jews on its own initiative, and later its police helped to deport them. French people also saved many.
points: The first Statute on Jews of October 1940 was issued without any German demand. It excluded Jews from public service and many professions, so thousands lost their livelihoods.

A second statute followed in June 1941. The Commissariat-General for Jewish Questions was set up in March 1941, first led by Xavier Vallat, and Jewish businesses were 'aryanised', that is taken over. Foreign Jews were interned in camps.
From 1942 Vichy's police, under Rene Bousquet's agreements with the SS, carried out arrests in both zones. Foreign Jews in the southern zone were handed over in August 1942.
On 16-17 July 1942, in the Vel' d'Hiv round-up, French police arrested about 13,000 Jews in Paris, including about 4,000 children.
Families were held in the Vélodrome d'Hiver cycling stadium and then sent through camps such as Drancy, a transit camp near Paris, to Auschwitz.
About 76,000 Jews were deported from France and about 2,500 survived. About three-quarters of the Jews in France survived the war, many helped by ordinary people and churches.
There is more on the wider Holocaust in the notes on anti-Semitism and the Holocaust.
notes.tip: Say that the first statute of October 1940 was Vichy's own, not German, and give the Vel' d'Hiv figures with 'about'.

notes.h: The Milice and compulsory labour
notes.b: By 1943 Vichy was becoming a police state. It created its own armed force and sent French workers to Germany.
points: The Milice, led by Joseph Darnand, was founded in January 1943. It was Vichy's paramilitary police, so French men hunted fellow French resisters and Jews and fought the maquis.
It carried out reprisals against civilians, which was a sign of Vichy becoming a police state by 1943-44.
The Service du Travail Obligatoire (STO), a compulsory labour service, was introduced in February 1943 after the voluntary relève had failed. It sent young French men to work in Germany.
Many went into hiding in the maquis to avoid it, which swelled the Resistance.
Vichy's police and administration carried out many arrests and deportations, so French officials were directly involved, and collaboration extended to the economy, with supplies sent to Germany.
Historians since Robert Paxton's Vichy France of 1972 have argued that Vichy's collaboration was active and not merely a shield against harsher German policy.

notes.h: De Gaulle and the Free French
notes.b: Resistance means organised opposition to the occupier and to Vichy. It began outside France, with a single general in London.
points: Charles de Gaulle, a brigadier-general and Under-Secretary for War in Reynaud's government in June 1940, broadcast an appeal on the BBC from London on 18 June 1940, calling on the French to continue the fight.
Churchill recognised him as leader of the Free French on 28 June 1940. French Equatorial Africa, led by Chad, rallied to him in August 1940.
His Free French forces fought alongside the British.
His relations with Churchill and especially Roosevelt, who preferred General Henri Giraud, were difficult.
De Gaulle won control of the French Committee of National Liberation, formed in Algiers in June 1943, and it became the Provisional Government of the French Republic in June 1944.
notes.tip: Distinguish the Free French (de Gaulle's forces outside France) from the internal Resistance and from the FFI, the 1944 union of armed resistance inside France.

notes.h: The internal Resistance and Jean Moulin
notes.b: Inside France resistance began with small groups and grew into an organised movement, which depended on the Communists and on Jean Moulin to unite it.
points: In 1940-41 the early groups were small and made up of volunteers. They produced underground newspapers, ran escape lines for Allied airmen and gathered intelligence for Britain.
In the south the main movements were Combat (Henri Frenay), Libération (Emmanuel d'Astier de La Vigerie) and Franc-Tireur.
The Communists joined armed resistance after Germany invaded the USSR on 22 June 1941. The Francs-Tireurs et Partisans, formed in 1942, became one of the largest armed groups.
The Germans took hostages and shot them in reprisal, for example at Châteaubriant in October 1941, hoping to frighten people away from resistance.
The Resistance was divided among Gaullists, Communists and other political groups, so unity was hard.

Jean Moulin, de Gaulle's representative, was parachuted into France in January 1942 and united the main groups. He chaired the first meeting of the National Council of the Resistance in Paris on 27 May 1943.
Moulin was arrested at Caluire near Lyon in June 1943 and died after torture in July 1943. The Council's programme of March 1944 set out plans for post-war social reform.
notes.tip: Resistance included underground newspapers, intelligence, escape lines, sabotage and the armed maquis. Say it was always a minority.

notes.h: The maquis, reprisals and rescue
notes.b: In 1943-44 armed resistance grew, and the Germans and the Milice answered with terror. Ordinary people also took risks to save others.
points: The maquis, groups of guerrillas in rural areas, grew as young men fled the STO in 1943 and 1944. In 1944 the armed groups were united as the French Forces of the Interior (FFI).
Sabotage of railways and telephone lines helped the Normandy landings, because it slowed German reinforcements. The Vercors maquis was crushed in July 1944.
The Gestapo and Milice used torture and executions, and Klaus Barbie was the Gestapo chief in Lyon.
On 9 June 1944 the SS Das Reich division hanged 99 men at Tulle, and on 10 June it massacred more than 600 villagers at Oradour-sur-Glane (642 is the usual figure).
The village of Le Chambon-sur-Lignon, where Protestant villagers led by Pastor André Trocmé sheltered thousands of Jews and refugees, became a symbol of civilian rescue.
The Resistance was always a minority, as was active collaboration. Most people tried to survive (attentisme, 'wait and see').
notes.tip: Use Oradour as the example of reprisals and Le Chambon as the example of rescue. Do not give a number for members of the Resistance.

notes.h: Liberation, 1944
notes.b: Allied landings and a rising in Paris freed France in 1944.
points: D-Day was on 6 June 1944, and there were landings in Provence on 15 August 1944, in which French forces under General de Lattre de Tassigny took part.

The Paris rising began on 19 August, and General Leclerc's 2nd Armoured Division, a Free French unit, entered the city. The German commander von Choltitz surrendered, and Paris was liberated on 25 August 1944.
On 26 August 1944 de Gaulle walked down the Champs-Élysées as head of the Provisional Government.
The Allies recognised his Provisional Government in October 1944. It prevented civil war between Gaullists and Communists and restored the Republic's authority.

notes.h: The purge, the trials and the new Republic
notes.b: After the liberation France settled accounts with collaborators. It then wrote a new constitution, and Vichy was finally buried.
points: In the purge (the épuration) there were summary executions of collaborators, about 9,000-10,000 though estimates vary, and women accused of relations with Germans were publicly shaved.
Resistance groups also carried out executions of collaborators and informers, and these reprisals were a source of political tension. Trials followed.
Pétain was sentenced to death in August 1945, but de Gaulle commuted the sentence to life imprisonment. Laval was shot on 15 October 1945.
An ordinance of April 1944 gave women the vote, first used in 1945.
De Gaulle resigned on 20 January 1946, and the Fourth Republic's constitution was approved by referendum in October 1946.

notes.h: Judging Vichy: shield, sword and memory
notes.b: How the French remembered Vichy changed over time. After the war a comforting myth took hold, and later historians and film-makers challenged it.
points: After the war the 'sword and shield' view held that de Gaulle was the sword and Pétain the shield (Robert Aron, History of Vichy, 1954).
Robert Paxton (Vichy France: Old Guard and New Order, 1972) argued that collaboration was Vichy's own choice and its anti-Jewish laws were home-grown.

The Gaullist myth of a nation united in resistance, which suited a country eager to forget, was challenged from the 1970s by Marcel Ophuls's film The Sorrow and the Pity (made 1969, shown in French cinemas in 1971, banned from French television until 1981) and by Paxton.
Henry Rousso's The Vichy Syndrome (1987) studied how France struggled to face this past.
Maurice Papon, a Vichy official, was convicted in 1998, and in a speech on 16 July 1995 President Jacques Chirac acknowledged the French state's responsibility for the Vel' d'Hiv round-up.
notes.tip: Examiners expect a judgement on Vichy (willing collaboration, Paxton) and on the Resistance (a minority but important).

notes.h: Assessment: the Third Republic, Vichy and France 1920-1945
notes.b: Judgements of the Third Republic weigh its survival and its reforms against its instability and its failure to resist invasion. Judgements of Vichy and the Resistance depend on whether you take the contemporary or the later view.
points: Achievement: the Third Republic stabilised the franc under Poincaré, survived the Depression and the leagues' challenge in 1934 without a coup, and its institutions held until 1940.
Limit: governments changed very often, the response to the Depression was slow, and France stayed divided. The failure to modernise the army left it unprepared for the German attack of 1940.
Achievement: the Popular Front brought paid holidays and shorter working hours to French workers in 1936.
Limit: the Popular Front's economic policies failed to reduce unemployment, the 40-hour week was undone in 1938, and it could not agree on how to respond to the Spanish Civil War.
Contemporary view: many French conservatives in 1940 saw the armistice and Pétain's rule as a necessary response to military defeat and the failures of the republic, and Pétain as a shield.
Later view: historians stress that Vichy was not forced into collaboration, and that its anti-Jewish policies went beyond German demands in some areas.
The Resistance was a minority but important, and it helped the Republic return in 1944-46.
Verdict: the problems were overcome only in part. Finance, survival of the Republic and social reform were achievements, but instability, division and defence were not solved before defeat in 1940.
notes.tip: A 'how far' question needs a stated verdict in the introduction and conclusion. Organise by problem (war legacy and finance, instability, the Depression, the leagues, defence and defeat, occupation and Vichy) and say for each whether it was overcome.

keyTerms.definition: A system of government in which power rests with elected representatives or with the people, protected by free elections and the rule of law.
Cooperation with an occupying power, in France the policy of the Vichy regime of working with Germany after 1940.
Organised opposition to an occupying power or a regime, including sabotage, intelligence gathering, propaganda and armed action.
The alliance of Socialists, Communists and Radicals in France, which won the 1936 election under Léon Blum.
The authoritarian state set up by Pétain in July 1940 in the unoccupied south of France, which collaborated with Germany.
The name given by the Vichy regime to its programme of authoritarian and conservative reform.
The paramilitary force founded by Vichy in January 1943 to hunt members of the Resistance.
The chain of fortifications built along the German border between 1929 and 1938 to protect France from attack.
The 1924 coalition of Radicals and Socialists under Édouard Herriot, which fell in 1925 after a financial crisis.
Right-wing paramilitary movements of the 1920s and 1930s, such as the Croix-de-Feu and Action française, that attacked the parliamentary republic.
The June 1936 settlement between employers and unions under Blum that ended the sit-down strikes and gave pay rises and collective bargaining.
The movement led by General de Gaulle from London from June 1940 that continued the war against Germany and Vichy.
